title: Marfan Syndrome: A Visual Guide to Connective Tissue Pathology
summary: Marfan syndrome is a systemic, autosomal dominant disorder of connective tissue caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene. It is characterized by specific ocular, cardiovascular, and skeletal manifestations that require lifelong monitoring.

sections.title: Ocular Hallmarks
content: Ectopia Lentis: Classic Upward and Superotemporal subluxation of the crystalline lens.
Zonular Integrity: Stretched or broken zonules (fibrillin-rich fibers).
Cornea Plana: Characteristically flat corneal curvature.
Increased Axial Length: Leading to high axial myopia.
Iris Hypoplasia: Resulting in transillumination defects and poor pupillary dilation.
Ciliary Body Hypoplasia: Often observed on ultrasound biomicroscopy.
Vitreous Liquefaction: Premature vitreous syneresis.

sections.title: Major Systemic Involvement
content: Cardiovascular: Aortic root aneurysm, Aortic dissection, Mitral valve prolapse (MVP).
Skeletal: Arachnodactyly (spider fingers), Pectus excavatum or carinatum, Scoliosis.
Integumentary: Striae atrophicae (stretch marks) without weight change.
Pulmonary: Spontaneous pneumothorax, apical blebs.
Dural Ectasia: Widening of the dural sac in the lumbosacral spine.

sections.title: Red Flag Complications
content: Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (High Risk due to axial length and vitreous changes)
Aortic Dissection (Life-threatening emergency)
Secondary Glaucoma (Angle-closure due to lens subluxation or pupillary block)
Presenile Cataracts (Nuclear sclerosis)
Endophthalmitis (Increased risk if lens surgery is required)

sections.title: Diagnostic Pathway: Ghent Criteria
content: Step 1: Clinical Evaluation of Systemic Score (>7 points).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam to confirm Ectopia Lentis.
Step 3: Echocardiography to measure Aortic Root Z-score.
Step 4: Molecular Genetic Testing for FBN1 mutation.
Step 5: Review Family History of Marfan Syndrome.

sections.title: Exhaustive Overview of Marfan
sections.content: Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a pervasive multi-system genetic disorder. In the eye, the classic finding of ectopia lentis occurs because the zonular fibers, composed of fibrillin-1, are weak or absent. This leads to the lens being pulled toward the strongest remaining zonules, typically in a superior-temporal direction. Beyond the eye, the cardiovascular implications are the most life-threatening, particularly aortic root dilation which can lead to rupture. Skeletal features like a high-arched palate and joint hypermobility are common. Management requires a multidisciplinary team including ophthalmologists, cardiologists, and geneticists. Regular dilated fundus exams are mandatory to monitor for retinal tears and detachments, which occur at a higher frequency in this population due to increased axial length and collagen defects.
